[exc_3af200c915ae90_11_v2] Chinese Contract Law — Chapter 1 General principles of contract law › Activity 1.1 › 1.2 Historical development of Chinese contract law › 1.2.1 Historical developments in other jurisdictions (pages 9)
roles: introduction | topics: chinese-contract-law-history | figures: fig_3af200c915ae90_73_v2
teaches: Surveys Hammurabi, Roman contract and tort distinctions, French and German codification, English common law, and the rise of freedom of contract.
scope: Historical comparative background across ancient Mesopotamia, Roman law, Continental Europe, and England. It is not an account of China's legal development or current law. The final English case quotation continues in excerpt 12.
Source context (scope explains when needed): exc_3af200c915ae90_12_v2
Roman law for the first time distinguished breaches of contract from tortious acts. Prior to that, as in ancient Greece, non-performance was simply regarded as infringement. Various provisions of the Roman law have become the origin of modern contract law in Continental Europe, based on which the French Civil Code (Code Civil des Franςais 1804) and the German Civil Code (Bürgerliches Gesetzbuch) were drafted. The French Civil Code established for the first time the principle of freedom of contract, which has become the core principle of modern contract law.

In England, the principles of modern contract law were well developed in common law courts in the early 19th century. The first important treatise expounding the English law of contract was arguably John Powell’s Essay upon the Law of Contracts and Agreements. The concept of freedom of contract, originating in the work of Adam Smith, was well summed up in the words of a judge in 1875 in the case of Printing and Numerical Registering Co. v. Sampson (1875) LR 19 Eq 462:

[exc_3af200c915ae90_14_v2] Chinese Contract Law — “ › 1.2.2 Historical developments in China › 8 (pages 11)
roles: introduction | topics: chinese-contract-law-history
teaches: Traces China's civil and contract-law history from the late Qing draft and 1930 Republican code through failed PRC codification, piecemeal 1980s statutes, and the 1999 Contract Law.
scope: Historical account centered on China through the 2009 textbook's 1999 Contract Law framework. Its claim that the GPCL was enacted in 1985 and its description of a civil code as still being drafted are preserved as source-period statements, not current law. Excerpt 13 supplies the opening debate over civil law in Imperial China.
Source context (scope explains when needed): exc_3af200c915ae90_13_v2
The three pieces of legislation on contract law were not intended to be a comprehensive set. They were enacted piecemeal to solve the immediate needs of the economic reform starting from 1979. They contained contradictory provisions, and the scope of each of them overlapped. In 1993, the drafting process of a new Contract Law started, which was intended to replace the three pieces of legislation. It is believed that the drafters of the new Contract Law, consisting of many legal academics this time, had made extensive reference to various sources, such as the UNIDROIT Principles of International Commercial Contracts (PICC) (http://www.unidroit.org/english/principles/contracts/main.htm),the United Nations Convention on Contracts for International Sale of Goods (CISG) (http://www.uncitral.org/uncitral/en/uncitral_texts/sale_goods.html), the Principles of European Contract Law (PECL) (http://frontpage.cbs.dk/law/commission_on_european_contract_law/), the civil codes of France and Germany, and the English common law. It was passed on 15 March 1999, effective 1 October 1999, and was supplemented by the Interpretation on Several Issues Regarding the Application of the Contract Law (1) (http://www.sjzmbc.gov.cn/en/public/englishshow.jsp?id=20060904158511) issued by the Supreme People’s Court and some other judicial interpretations on technology contract and construction contract.

[exc_3af200c915ae90_9_v2] Chinese Contract Law — Chapter 1 General principles of contract law › Activity 1.1 › 5 (pages 8)
roles: introduction | topics: chinese-contract-law-history
teaches: Explains how merchant tribunals and lex mercatoria entered English and U.S. common law, then contrasts reputation-based enforcement in Western jurisdictions with the source's assessment of commercial dispute resolution in China.
scope: Historical comparative background, not a chronology of Chinese legislation. Claims that business ethics in China had yet to be cultivated, judgment enforcement was immature, and many disputes used non-legal means are the 2009 textbook's characterizations, not current findings.
In the US, merchants had tried to avoid the time-consuming court procedures for resolving commercial disputes until the end of the 18th century. Similar to the situation in England, the outcome of the competition between courts of law and merchants’ tribunals was that the customs of merchants were absorbed by judges and integrated into the common law.

The experience in Western jurisdictions shows that merchants’ concern about their goodwill and long-term reputation, rather than the effectiveness of the court system, is probably the biggest driving force behind the enforceability of contracts. In China, however, business ethics have yet to be cultivated. The deterrent force of peer pressure on contract breakers remains to be seen. Coupled with the immature system of the enforcement of court judgments, it is hardly surprising that many commercial disputes in China are resolved by non-legal means.

In the next section of the unit, you will find out more about the key milestones in the historical development of Chinese contract law.

[exc_3af200c915ae90_42_v2] Chinese Contract Law — “ › Case Study 1.3 › 18 (pages 21)
roles: exercise, worked_example | topics: chinese-contract-concept-and-scope | figures: fig_3af200c915ae90_216_v2
Scope not reviewed. Check the source's applicability before using it.
In Continental civil law jurisdictions such as Germany, Japan, France, Switzerland and Italy, the contract law is found within the civil code or the code of obligations. Contract law, tort law and the law of unjust enrichment are all regarded as part of the law of obligations.

At the time of writing, China’s civil code is still in the drafting stage. The General Principles of Civil Law and the Contract Law remain the sources of Chinese contract law. In addition, the Sino-foreign Equity Joint Venture Law and the Sino-Foreign Cooperative Joint Venture Law contain specific provisions on Sino-foreign joint venture contracts.

Administrative rules and regulations also constitute sources of the Chinese contract law. Furthermore, according to article 125 of the Contract Law, ‘transaction practices’ may also be the so urces of contract law.

title: Historical Development of Chinese Contract Law
content:
# Historical Development of Chinese Contract Law

*Based on the open textbook **Chinese Contract Law**, Chapter 1 (§1.2.2). The account reflects the book's 2009 perspective; statements such as "the civil code is still being drafted" are source-period claims, not current law.*

## 1. Imperial China (pre-1911): no civil code
- Whether Imperial China had "civil law" (as opposed to criminal law) is **debatable**: Liang Chichao (梁啟超) and Wang Boqi (王伯琦) argued it did not exist; Yang Honglie (楊鴻烈) held the opposite view.
- Beyond dispute: **no civil code ever existed** in Imperial China, though there was separate legislation on **marriage and debt**.

## 2. Late Qing: first draft civil code
- **1902**: Emperor Guang Xu formed a team to draft a civil code modelled on Continental European codes.
- Drafting ran **1908–1910**, producing the **Draft Civil Law of Great Qing (《大清民律草案》)** — the first civil code in China's history, though only in draft form.
- **Never enacted**: the Qing Dynasty was overthrown shortly afterwards.

## 3. Republican era: first enacted civil code
- **April 1927**: National Government established; **December 1928**: Legislative Yuan put in charge of drafting.
- **January 1929**: Drafting Committee of the Civil Code set up; compilation began February 1929.
- **26 December 1930**: the **Civil Law of the Republic of China (《中華民國民法》)** promulgated — the first enacted civil code in China's history, containing **detailed contract law provisions**.

## 4. PRC: failed codification, then piecemeal statutes
- After 1949, drafting of a new civil code began in **1954**; a draft was completed in **December 1956**, but enactment was derailed by the antirightist movements and the Cultural Revolution.
- Political unrest halted in **1978**; rather than revisit the old draft, China started over with **three separate contract statutes**, enacted piecemeal to meet the immediate needs of economic reform from 1979:
  - **Economic Contract Law (1981)**
  - **Foreign Economic Contract Law (1985)**
  - **Technology Contract Law (1987)**
- The **General Principles of Civil Law (GPCL, 1985)** is *not* a civil code — only "general principles," like the introductory chapter of a code still in drafting.
- The three statutes were not comprehensive: they contained **contradictory provisions** and **overlapping scopes**.

## 5. The 1999 Contract Law
- **1993**: drafting of a unified Contract Law began, intended to replace the three statutes; drafters were largely legal academics.
- Extensive reference to international and comparative sources: **UNIDROIT PICC**, **CISG**, **Principles of European Contract Law (PECL)**, the **French and German civil codes**, and **English common law**.
- **Passed 15 March 1999, effective 1 October 1999**; supplemented by the Supreme People's Court's *Interpretation on Several Issues Regarding the Application of the Contract Law (1)* and other judicial interpretations on technology and construction contracts.

## Quick timeline
| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| pre-1911 | No civil code; separate marriage/debt legislation only |
| 1908–1910 | Draft Civil Law of Great Qing (never enacted) |
| 1930 | Civil Law of the Republic of China promulgated |
| 1954–1956 | PRC civil code draft (not enacted) |
| 1981 / 1985 / 1987 | Economic / Foreign Economic / Technology Contract Laws |
| 1985 | General Principles of Civil Law |
| 1993 | New unified Contract Law drafting begins |
| 1999 | Contract Law passed (15 Mar) and effective (1 Oct) |
